questions.question: A research task has independent questions and one final report. What team structure lets work happen concurrently and then be combined?
options: One agent reads every source sequentially in a single context
A lead plans, delegates to workers, and synthesizes their results
Workers choose unrelated tasks without a shared plan
A fixed pipeline sends every question to the same worker
questions.explanation: Independent questions can fan out to focused workers at the same time, then a lead combines their results into one report. A single serial reader loses that overlap and keeps all source material in one growing context.

questions.question: Why does a subagent's fresh context help in the supervisor pattern?
options: It gives the worker access to every other worker's raw transcript
It removes the need for a focused sub-question
It makes the worker's answer deterministic across model versions
It avoids carrying the lead's long planning and history context
questions.explanation: A fresh worker context contains its scoped sub-question without the lead’s accumulated planning and conversation history. Giving it every peer’s raw transcript would reintroduce context pollution rather than preserve a clean work area.

questions.question: Three independent workers take 0.3 seconds each. Ignoring plan and synthesis time, what does the lesson predict for concurrent wall time?
options: Roughly 0.6 seconds, because two workers are required
Roughly 1.2 seconds, because the lead waits twice
Roughly 0.3 seconds, near the slowest worker
Roughly 0.9 seconds, because durations add in parallel
questions.explanation: When three independent workers run concurrently for 0.3 seconds each, the worker portion finishes near the maximum duration: max(0.3, 0.3, 0.3)=0.3 seconds. The 0.9-second choice adds their times as if they ran sequentially; planning and synthesis are excluded by the prompt.

questions.question: The lead decomposes a research question into sub-questions that omit the user's main concern. Which failure mode is this?
options: A worker's fresh context is too large
The lead hallucinates an incomplete plan
An activity replays a cached result
A reviewer silently changes the benchmark
questions.explanation: If the lead omits the user’s central concern, the decomposition plan is incomplete before workers start. A worker can still have a clean context and execute its assigned sub-question accurately, yet the system will miss the requested goal.

questions.question: Two workers return contradictory facts. What should the lead do in its synthesis?
options: Average the two claims into one unsupported conclusion
Surface the disagreement or request a targeted follow-up
Choose whichever answer was returned last without noting it
Delete both results and report that no workers ran
questions.explanation: The lead should preserve the contradiction or ask a targeted follow-up, because selecting the last result uses arrival order rather than evidence. Averaging incompatible factual claims can also manufacture a conclusion neither worker supported.

questions.question: A task's second step cannot begin until the first step returns its output. Which topology is the better fit?
options: An LLM selector that chooses a worker at random
A full shared pool that lets all workers speak at once
A larger supervisor team with more simultaneous workers
A sequential pipeline rather than parallel supervisor fan-out
questions.explanation: A strict dependency means step two cannot be formed until step one returns its output, so work should flow sequentially. More simultaneous workers do not remove the dependency; they simply wait or receive missing inputs.
